Neonates of the spotted skink (Carinascincus ocellatus) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of 3 cm [Lb = 3 cm], a relatively small size for a skink of the Carinascincus genus. This modest body dimension at the onset of independent life, generally observed following a gestation period where embryos develop within the oviduct, reflects a life-history strategy that balances litter size against offspring investment. Field studies have noted that the pronounced yolk absorption completed during the later stages of embryonic development provides the newly emerged individuals with sufficient endogenous resources to begin exploring their cool, damp Tasmanian habitats without the immediate need for prey capture. The reproductive cycle of this species is tightly constrained by the cool-temperate climate it inhabits, and at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the duration of embryonic development leading to the hatching event is recorded as 87 days [ab = 87 days]. This protracted incubation, equivalent to roughly 12 to 13 weeks, is a direct physiological response to the low thermal regime and positions the species among slower-developing lygosomine skinks. The birth length of 3 cm [Lb = 3 cm] is therefore not merely a static measurement but a product of the interaction between maternal provisioning and local thermal conditions.

As juvenile individuals transition into the sub-adult phase, they undergo a consistent period of somatic growth that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity. Data from mark-recapture studies on populations in northeastern Tasmania indicate that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activation and the ability to engage in reproductive activities, occurs when females have reached a snout-vent length of 5.1 cm [Lp = 5.1 cm]. This threshold size appears to be a reliable indicator of physiological readiness, as it correlates with the development of vitellogenic follicles in the ovaries. Males, while maturing at a slightly smaller average size compared to females, still typically require the same linear dimension to initiate spermatogenesis and exhibit the courtship behaviors necessary for successful cloacal copulation. The age at which this size is achieved is highly dependent on the local thermal microclimate and the availability of invertebrate prey, with individuals in cooler, high-altitude sites often taking an additional year to cross this developmental milestone compared to their counterparts in warmer coastal areas. Reaching this 5.1 cm [Lp = 5.1 cm] snout-vent length represents a significant energetic investment, as the lizard must allocate resources towards both structural growth and the accumulation of sufficient fat reserves to support the coming reproductive effort.

Upon reaching sexual maturity, the body size of the spotted skink continues to increase, albeit at a decelerating rate, until an asymptotic maximum is approached. The ultimate snout-vent length for females in this species is recorded as 8.1 cm [Li = 8.1 cm], a size that is generally attained after several years of post-pubertal growth and is associated with the highest rates of reproductive output. Males, in contrast, reach a slightly smaller final size, plateauing at an ultimate snout-vent length of 7.9 cm [Li = 7.9 cm]. This subtle but consistent sexual dimorphism in overall body size is thought to reflect differential selective pressures; selection may favor larger body size in females to maximize abdominal volume for carrying a clutch of up to four shelled eggs, while males, which engage in active mate searching and combat, may benefit from a more streamlined and agile morphology. The maximum recorded wet weight for fully-grown, gravid females in the population is approximately 12 grams [Wwi = approximately 12 grams], a mass that includes the developing clutch. This relationship between linear size and mass is consistent with the general allometric scaling observed in other small, viviparous Australian skinks.

The reproductive output of the spotted skink, while modest, is finely tuned to the resource availability of its environment. Each year, a sexually mature female that has successfully mated and stored sperm within her reproductive tract will produce approximately 2 to 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 litters per year], with litter sizes ranging from one to four young [N_R_i = litter sizes ranging from one to four young]. This annual reproductive strategy, where multiple broods are produced per year, is common among reptiles inhabiting temperate zones with short active seasons. The actual number of offspring in a given litter is strongly correlated with the female's body condition and her snout-vent length, with larger individuals typically producing the maximum of four offspring. This per-event fecundity, combined with the annual cycle, represents the maximum reproductive rate achievable under the cool thermal conditions of the species' habitat. At a controlled temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], which is typical of the soil temperatures experienced during key vitellogenic periods in spring, the physiological machinery supporting gestation proceeds at a slow but steady pace. This combination of approximately 2 to 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 litters per year] and small brood sizesnan ensures that each offspring receives adequate maternal investment through the lengthy gestation.

Longevity in this species, as with many small ectotherms, is influenced by the rate of metabolism, which is directly tied to environmental temperature. Under natural conditions, the oldest documented individuals from long-term field surveys have achieved a maximum lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when maintained at a baseline thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan for a small-bodied skink, which contrasts with the shorter lives of many low-latitude lizards, is a classic outcome of a "slow" life-history pace. The low metabolic rates and reduced activity periods associated with the cool Tasmanian climate likely contribute to reduced cellular damage accumulation over time, delaying the onset of senescence and age-related physiological deterioration.
